extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and induction
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and exposition of the philosophical foundations of induction and causation, defining what counts as a cause and what grounds inductive certainty. Focuses on the nature of causes (positive/negative conditions), the universality of causation, and the role of rigorous laws (number/space) vs. laws of succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Causation (universality)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a universal truth that every fact which has a beginning has a cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This law is presented as coextensive with the entire field of successive phenomena and as the fundamental law required for a Logic of Induction. It is the candidate law of succession possessing indefeasibility analogous to geometric truths; recognition of this law makes reduction of inductive process to rules possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause defined as assemblage of all conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause, philosophically speaking, is the sum total of the conditions, positive and negative, taken together; the whole of the contingencies of every description which, being realized, the consequent invariably follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy requires enumerating all conditions; in practice some may be omitted when understood or irrelevant. Negative conditions are usually summarized as the absence of counteracting causes. Examples: death after eating a dish depends on food + constitution + health + atmospheric state; real cause is entire set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative conditions cannot produce effects (are absences)
rubrics_metrics.description: From nothing, from a mere negation, no consequences can proceed; negative conditions are not producing causes but indicate absence of preventing causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although ordinary language sometimes treats negations as 'causes' (e.g., sentinel off post causing surprise), scientifically negative conditions are logically different and should be handled as absence of counteracting causes. For practical brevity negative conditions may be summed up under one head.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to single out proximate antecedent as 'cause' (but incomplete)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is common to single out one only of the antecedents under the denomination of Cause, calling the others merely Conditions; often the one nominated is the antecedent which came last into existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical/linguistic convenience (e.g., ‘eating the dish’ named cause of death), but philosophically incorrect: any such singled-out condition is usually only part of the full assemblage of antecedents. The statement of cause is incomplete unless all relevant conditions are introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate all conditions for accurate causal statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of the cause is incomplete, unless in some shape or other we introduce all the conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming at accuracy, one should enumerate all positive conditions and consider the single negative condition (absence of counteracting causes). Omission is only tolerable when conditions are implicitly understood or irrelevant to the purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of number and space: rigorous universality but limited to simultaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of number and the theorems of geometry are examples of rigorous universality; laws of number are common to synchronous and successive phenomena, but laws of extension and figure are laws of simultaneous phenomena only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although these laws are the type of certainty desired for inductive foundations, they cannot by themselves yield laws of succession; from laws of space and number alone nothing can be deduced except other laws of space and number. They must be combined with premises about succession to yield temporal uniformities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a law of succession with indefeasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: For inductive logic we must find some law of succession which resembles geometric truths in never being defeated or suspended by any change of circumstances; this fundamental law is the Law of Causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an indefeasible law provides the foundation and test for verifying other inductive generalizations; it is by reference to such universal inductions that weaker inductions may be elevated to laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductions corroborate or refute one another by ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: All inductions which can be connected together by a ratiocination are confirmatory of one another; any which lead deductively to incompatible consequences become mutually each other's test, showing that one or other must be given up or more guardedly expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inductions confirm each other, the derived induction attains at least the certainty of the weakest premise; scientific experiments (e.g., Torricelli) can strengthen and convert doubtful generalizations into well-established doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation notion for induction must be empirical/physical, not metaphysical
rubrics_metrics.description: The only notion of a cause which the theory of induction requires is such a notion as can be gained from experience; causes considered are physical (phenomenal) causes, not ontological or efficient causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis avoids metaphysical disputes about efficient causes; inductive logic needs only the empirical recognition that invariability of succession holds between facts and antecedent facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent vs patient distinction is verbal and not philosophically fundamental
rubrics_metrics.description: Although ordinary language distinguishes agent (that which acts) and patient (that which is acted upon), the distinction vanishes on examination: patients are also agents in many phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in sensations the outward object and the organs are co‑operative; in poisoning both poison and vital properties of the patient are active. The supposed agent/patient dichotomy is a logical fiction of expression, not a deep metaphysical fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical naming of cause depends on rhetorical/purposive considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice the particular condition most conspicuous or most relevant to the immediate purpose is usually styled the cause (e.g., the casting vote called the cause of legislation's effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such naming is often for responsibility, convenience or emphasis; scientific discourse should avoid this caprice and aim to specify the full assemblage of conditions where accuracy is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes often involve conjunctions of antecedents (positive conditions) and may require absence of counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is seldom that an invariable sequence subsists between a consequent and one single antecedent; usually the consequent depends on the concurrence of several antecedents, positive and negative (absence of counteracting causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific causal statements should recognize conjunctions of antecedents; negative conditions usually summarized as absence of counteracting causes are commonly needed in addition to the positive set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions and preventive agencies exist but are often assimilable
rubrics_metrics.description: There are a few exceptions where a property seems purely preventive (e.g., opacity intercepting light), which may appear to contradict summarizing negatives as absence of counteracting causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such exceptions need not affect practical application because they may be explainable by discovering other relations; even where preventive agencies seem different, the formula summing negatives remains practically useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: To elevate an induction to a law, show it is true or that a universal induction admits exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If we can show with respect to any induction that either it must be true, or one of the certain and universal inductions must admit of an exception, then the former generalization will attain the same absolute certainty and indefeasibleness within its bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the method proposed for making many inductions attain the status of laws of nature: demonstrate incompatibility with established universal inductions or show necessity of truth under those universals.
